mainTopic: Assessing a struck victim who improved and then died: רבי נחמיה vs. the רבנן, the sources for holding the striker in custody, and the start of the משנה on mistaken intent in murder
overview: Earlier, רבי נחמיה and the רבנן argued about a case where a striker's victim was expected to die, got better, and then got worse and died. רבי נחמיה says the striker is exempt, and he proves it from the words "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה". The רבנן use those words to teach that the striker is locked up until we know what happens to the victim. The גמרא then asks where each side learns this rule of custody. The מקושש cannot be the source, because he was surely liable to death. So רבי נחמיה learns it from the מגדף, whose guilt was unknown. The רבנן say the מגדף was a one-time ruling, and a ברייתא proves the difference between the two cases. Next the גמרא explains how each side uses the two 'assessments' in the פסוקים. It then quotes two ברייתות about reassessing an injured victim, and notes that the unnamed one follows רבי נחמיה. Finally a new משנה begins about a killer who meant to kill a target he would not be executed for, or meant to hit a spot where the blow could not kill.

steps.title: רבי נחמיה's proof from the verse: the striker is exempt
steps.stepSummary: The words "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה" would be obvious if read simply. So they must teach that if the victim got better and later died, the striker is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: "...upon his staff, then the one who struck is cleared." Could you really think that the victim is walking around the market and the striker gets executed? Rather, the verse means a case where they estimated he would die, he got better than he was, and afterwards he got worse and died. The verse teaches that the striker is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting רבי נחמיה's proof from the פסוק. He shows that the words "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה" must be teaching something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the victim is alive and walking, of course the striker is not killed, so the פסוק would not need to say so. רבי נחמיה therefore applies it to a harder case: the victim improved, walked around, and only later got worse and died. In that case the striker is פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: "The one who struck is cleared" (שמות 21:19)
His walking staff
They estimated that he would die
He got better ... he got worse
Exempt

steps.confusionAlert: This is רבי נחמיה's reading only. The רבנן hold the striker is liable in this case, and they read the same words differently (next steps).
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the base for the rest of the section. Since רבי נחמיה uses "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה" for this rule, the גמרא will ask what the רבנן do with those words.

phrases.english: "...upon his staff, then the one who struck is cleared."
phrases.notes: This is the end of the פסוק in שמות 21:19, "if he gets up and walks outside upon his staff."

phrases.english: Would it enter your mind
that this one (the victim) is walking in the market
and that one (the striker) is executed?
Rather, this is a case where they estimated him for death,
and he got better than he had been,
and afterwards he got worse and died –
that he (the striker) is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תַּעֲלֶה עַל דַּעְתְּךָ שֶׁזֶּה מְהַלֵּךְ בַּשּׁוּק וְזֶה נֶהֱרָג
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבי נחמיה's proof, which began before this section
steps.raayaObject: רבי נחמיה's ruling that the striker is exempt if the victim improved and later died
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 21:19, "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה", which would be obvious if read simply

steps.title: How do the רבנן use the words "the striker is cleared"?
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן do not learn רבי נחמיה's exemption from the verse, so what do those words teach them?
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן, what do they learn from "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the other side. The רבנן disagree with רבי נחמיה, so the words must teach them something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes that no words of the תורה are wasted. Since the רבנן hold the striker is liable in the 'got better then died' case, they need a different use for "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה".

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages, the majority opinion
What do they learn from it?

phrases.english: And the Rabbis, this "then the one who struck is cleared"
what do they learn from it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן, הַאי ״וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה״ מַאי דָּרְשִׁי בֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the other side uses the פסוק that רבי נחמיה just used
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the רבנן learn from "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה"

steps.title: The רבנן: the verse teaches that the striker is held in custody
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן learn from the verse that the striker is locked up while we wait to see what happens to the victim.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches that they lock him up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers. The רבנן learn חבישה (holding the striker in custody) from the words "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה".
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the תורה says the striker is "cleared" once the victim walks, then before that he must have been held. So the words teach that he is locked up until the victim's outcome is clear, and then he is released.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches
They lock him up / hold him in custody
Custody, being held while waiting

phrases.english: It teaches that they lock him up.
phrases.notes: The "him" is the striker. "Cleared" then means he is let out of custody.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 2
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן learn from the verse that the striker is held in custody until the outcome is known

steps.title: Where does רבי נחמיה learn custody?
steps.stepSummary: רבי נחמיה used the verse for something else, so where does he get the rule of custody?
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי נחמיה, where does he learn custody from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks the reverse question. רבי נחמיה used the verse for his exemption, so where does he learn that the striker is locked up?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes both sides agree to the rule of חבישה. The only question is which source each side uses for it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where does he know it?

phrases.english: And Rabbi Nechemya, custody, from where does he learn it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors step 2, asking the same kind of question about רבי נחמיה

steps.title: רבי נחמיה learns custody from the wood gatherer
steps.stepSummary: רבי נחמיה learns custody from the מקושש, who was held under guard.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from the wood gatherer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי נחמיה learns חבישה from the מקושש, the man who gathered wood on שבת in the desert and was held under guard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה says of the מקושש "וַיַּנִּיחוּ אֹתוֹ בַּמִּשְׁמָר" (במדבר 15:34). רבי נחמיה learns from there that a person whose case is undecided may be held, so he does not need "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה" for this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: He learns (it) from
The wood gatherer who broke שבת in the desert (במדבר 15)

phrases.english: He learns it from the wood gatherer.
phrases.notes: במדבר 15:34, where they put him "under guard."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 4
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי נחמיה learns חבישה from the story of the מקושש

steps.title: Why don't the רבנן also learn from the wood gatherer?
steps.stepSummary: If the מקושש is a good source, the רבנן could learn custody from there too, and "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה" would be free to teach רבי נחמיה's exemption.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן too, let them learn it from the wood gatherer!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the רבנן. Why do they need the verse for custody if the מקושש already teaches it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the רבנן could learn חבישה from the מקושש, then "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה" would have nothing left to teach them. They would then have to accept רבי נחמיה's reading. So the challenge threatens the רבנן's position.

keyTerms.meaning: Also, too
Let them learn it

phrases.english: And the Rabbis too, let them learn it from the wood gatherer!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רבי נחמיה's source from step 5 to challenge the רבנן's reading in step 3
steps.kashyaTarget: The רבנן's use of "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה" for חבישה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Custody can already be learned from the מקושש, so the verse would be unneeded for it

steps.title: The wood gatherer's case is different
steps.stepSummary: The מקושש was surely liable to death, and only the method was unknown. The striker might not be liable at all, so you cannot learn his custody from the מקושש.
steps.simpleTranslation: The wood gatherer was definitely liable to death, and משה just did not know which death penalty applied. That excludes this striker, where we do not know whether he is liable to death or not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the רבנן by showing that the מקושש is not like the striker.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Locking up the מקושש made sense because he was certainly going to be executed; the only open question was how. The striker may turn out to be innocent if the victim lives. So the רבנן hold that a separate פסוק is needed to allow holding him, and that פסוק is "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה".

keyTerms.meaning: Someone liable to death
By which method he should be executed
To exclude, unlike
We do not know

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree the striker is held in custody. The רבנן learn it from "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה", because the מקושש was surely liable to death and the striker may not be. The next step shows that this same problem pushes רבי נחמיה to learn custody from the מגדף instead, which leaves "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה" free for his exemption.
steps.confusionAlert: The question about the מקושש was never whether he was guilty; that was clear. It was only which death penalty to use. That is the whole difference from the striker.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer explains why the רבנן cannot accept רבי נחמיה's source, so the dispute between them stays standing.

phrases.english: The wood gatherer was liable to death,
and Moshe did not know
by what means he should be killed.
That excludes this one (the striker),

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא יָדְעִינַן אִי בַּר קְטָלָא הוּא
phrases.english: where we do not know if he is liable to death
or if he is not liable to death.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְקוֹשֵׁשׁ בַּר קְטָלָא הוּא, וּמֹשֶׁה לָא הֲוָה יָדַע קְטָלֵיהּ בְּמַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 6
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Custody of the מקושש could teach custody of any person whose case is undecided
steps.terutzMaskana: The מקושש was certainly liable to death and only the method was unknown, so his case cannot teach custody for a striker who may not be liable at all

steps.title: רבי נחמיה learns custody from the blasphemer
steps.stepSummary: The rule from step 7 seems to block רבי נחמיה too, so the גמרא shows he learns custody from the מגדף, where it was unknown whether he was liable to death at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי נחמיה learns it from the blasphemer. They did not know whether he deserved death, and still they locked him up.
steps.whatsHappening: Step 7 showed that the מקושש cannot be the source for locking up a striker. So the גמרא gives רבי נחמיה a different source: the מגדף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem with the מקושש was that his death penalty was certain, while the striker might not be liable at all. The מגדף fits better, because משה did not know if he was liable to death, and he was still held in custody. This is exactly like the striker, whose outcome is also unknown.

keyTerms.meaning: The blasphemer, the man who cursed ה' (ויקרא 24)
He learns (a law from a source)
Liable to be killed
They locked him up / held him under guard

steps.whyThisMatters: The case of the striker needs a source where the man held in custody might not be liable at all. The מגדף is that kind of case.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Nechemya learns it from the blasphemer,
phrases.notes: The question is left unsaid: after step 7, where does רבי נחמיה get the custody rule? This is the answer.

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא הֲוָה יָדַע אִי בַּר קְטָלָא הוּא,
phrases.english: since he did not know if he was liable to death,
phrases.notes: The "he" who did not know is משה.

phrases.english: and they locked him up.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 7 ruled out the מקושש as a source for the striker. That logic also knocks out רבי נחמיה's source from step 5, so here he gets a new one.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacing the source with a better-matching precedent
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי נחמיה, like the רבנן, would have no source for custody once the מקושש is ruled out.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי נחמיה learns custody from the מגדף, where it was not known whether he was liable to death at all.

steps.title: The רבנן treat the מגדף as a one-time ruling
steps.stepSummary: Why don't the רבנן also learn from the מגדף? They hold it was a הוראת שעה, a special ruling just for that moment.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן, why don't they learn from the blasphemer? They say the blasphemer was a one-time ruling for that moment only.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the רבנן don't also use the מגדף, and answers that they see it as a one-time ruling that cannot teach a general law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the מגדף were a normal source, the רבנן could learn custody from it and would not need the verse "וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה". The רבנן avoid this by saying that holding the מגדף was a special decision for that moment. You cannot build a permanent rule from a one-time ruling, so they still need the verse.

keyTerms.meaning: A one-time ruling for a specific moment, not a lasting law
The Sages (the majority view arguing with רבי נחמיה)

steps.confusionAlert: The word "וְרַבָּנַן" alone is the whole question here: "And what about the רבנן?" The answer comes right after.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis?
phrases.notes: He means: why don't the רבנן also learn custody from the blasphemer?

phrases.english: The blasphemer was a one-time ruling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that רבי נחמיה uses the מגדף, the גמרא checks why the רבנן don't use it too.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the רבנן do not learn custody from the מגדף.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן hold the מגדף was a הוראת שעה, so it cannot teach a general law.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the precedent: the מגדף was a one-time ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רבנן could learn custody from the מגדף, leaving 'וְנִקָּה הַמַּכֶּה' with nothing to teach them.
steps.terutzMaskana: For the רבנן, holding the מגדף was a הוראת שעה and teaches no general law, so they still need the verse for custody.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows the מקושש and the מגדף were different
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא proves that with the מקושש משה knew there was a death penalty and only lacked the method, while with the מגדף he did not know if there was a death penalty at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: משה knew the wood gatherer deserved death, because the תורה says "those who desecrate it shall be put to death." He only did not know which kind of death, as it says "for it had not been made clear." But about the blasphemer it says only "to make it clear to them by the word of ה'," because משה did not know if he deserved death at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up the difference it has been relying on between the מקושש and the מגדף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 7 and 8 depend on one idea: the מקושש was surely liable to death, but the מגדף might not have been. The ברייתא proves this from the wording of the פסוקים. For the מקושש the verse says only that the method was not clear ("מה יעשה לו"). For the מגדף it says only "to make it clear," which means the whole judgment was open.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught (in a ברייתא)
The wood gatherer who broke שבת (במדבר 15)
By which type of death penalty
At all

steps.whatToRemember: מקושש: certainly liable to death, only the method was unknown. מגדף: unknown whether he was liable to death at all. That is why only the מגדף resembles the striker.

phrases.english: As it was taught:
Moshe our teacher knew
that the wood gatherer was liable to death,
as it says: "Those who desecrate it shall surely be put to death,"
but he did not know
by which death he was to be killed,
as it says: "For it had not been made clear, etc."
phrases.notes: במדבר 15:34. The verse goes on: "what should be done to him," meaning only the method was unclear.

phrases.english: But about the blasphemer it does not say
anything except "to make it clear to them by the word of ה',"
because Moshe did not know

phrases.aramaic: אִם הוּא בֶּן מִיתָה כׇּל עִיקָּר אִם לָאו.
phrases.english: whether he was liable to death at all or not.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְתַנְיָא: יוֹדֵעַ הָיָה מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ שֶׁהַמְקוֹשֵׁשׁ בְּמִיתָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the difference between מקושש and מגדף that steps 7 and 8 rely on.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the מקושש was surely liable to death while the מגדף's liability was unknown.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא reading the wording of במדבר 15:34 ("כי לא פרש") against ויקרא 24:12 ("לפרש להם").

steps.title: Why do the רבנן need two assessments of the victim?
steps.stepSummary: For רבי נחמיה, the two assessments in the פסוקים teach two different cases. For the רבנן, the second assessment seems unnecessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for רבי נחמיה: that is why two assessments are written. In one case they assessed him for death and he lived. In the other they assessed him for death and he improved from how he was. But for the רבנן, why do I need two assessments?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the רבנן. It shows that רבי נחמיה can explain why the תורה describes the victim's condition twice, and asks what the רבנן do with the second description.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוקים (שמות 21:18-19) describe the victim being judged twice: first "he did not die but is bedridden," then "if he rises and walks outside." רבי נחמיה uses these for two exempt cases: one where the victim fully recovered, and one where he improved and then still died. The רבנן hold the striker is liable in the 'improved, then died' case, so they lose that second case, and it is unclear what the second assessment teaches them.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense (for one side), setting up a challenge to the other side
Assessment(s) of the victim's condition, judging whether he will die
They assessed him as likely to die
He got better / his condition eased

steps.confusionAlert: "בִּשְׁלָמָא" does not mean the גמרא agrees with רבי נחמיה. It is only setting up a challenge against the רבנן.

phrases.english: It makes sense according to Rabbi Nechemya,
that is why two assessments are written:
phrases.notes: שמות 21:18-19, "he did not die but is bedridden" and "if he rises and walks outside."

phrases.english: one, where they assessed him for death and he lived,
and one, where they assessed him for death
and he got better than he was.
phrases.notes: In this case he improves but later dies anyway.

phrases.english: But according to the Rabbis,
why do I need two assessments?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְרַבִּי נְחֶמְיָה, הַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיבִי תְּרֵי אוּמְדָּנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the sources for custody are settled, the גמרא turns to a new challenge against the רבנן based on the wording of the פסוקים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי נחמיה gives each of the two assessments its own exempt case. The רבנן reject the 'improved, then died' exemption, so they seem to have no case for the second assessment, which would make it extra wording.

steps.title: For the רבנן, the two assessments teach two different cases
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן use the two assessments for two cases. In one, the victim was expected to die but lived. In the other, he was expected to live but died.
steps.simpleTranslation: One assessment teaches the case where they judged he would die and he lived. The other teaches the case where they judged he would live and he died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 11. It shows that even for the רבנן, the second assessment is not wasted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each assessment in the פסוקים teaches its own case where the striker is not executed. In the first case, the victim was expected to die but recovered. In the second, he was expected to live but then died. So the רבנן also have a use for both assessments.

keyTerms.meaning: They assessed him, meaning the court estimated how serious the wound was
For death, meaning the wound was judged deadly
For life, meaning the wound was judged not deadly
And he died

phrases.english: One: they assessed him for death, and he lived;
and one: they assessed him for life, and he died.
phrases.notes: In both cases the striker is not put to death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 11 about the extra assessment for the רבנן.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the two assessments into two separate cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: For the רבנן the second assessment has no job
steps.terutzMaskana: For the רבנן, one assessment covers 'judged deadly but he lived' and the other covers 'judged not deadly but he died'

steps.title: Why רבי נחמיה needs no פסוק for 'judged to live, then died'
steps.stepSummary: רבי נחמיה does not need a פסוק for the case where the victim was judged to live and then died. The striker already left בית דין cleared.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי נחמיה? In the case where they judged he would live and he died, no פסוק is needed. The striker already went out of court innocent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where רבי נחמיה learns the case of 'judged to live, then died.' It answers that he does not need a פסוק for it at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once בית דין judged the wound not deadly, the striker walked out cleared of a death sentence. Logic alone says he is not brought back to be executed, so no פסוק is needed. That frees both assessments for רבי נחמיה to teach his own two cases.

keyTerms.meaning: No פסוק is needed, because it is known from logic
He left בית דין innocent

phrases.english: And Rabbi Nechemya?
phrases.notes: Short for: where does רבי נחמיה learn the case of 'judged to live, and he died'?

phrases.english: If they assessed him for life and he died,
no verse is needed,
since he already left the court innocent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the רבנן's use of both assessments is shown, the גמרא asks how רבי נחמיה covers the case of 'judged to live, then died.'
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Where does רבי נחמיה learn that the striker is not executed if the victim was judged to live and then died?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No פסוק is needed, because the striker already left בית דין innocent.

steps.title: A ברייתא on a victim who improved and then died
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules on a victim whose condition changed. רבי נחמיה says to follow the middle assessment. The חכמים say there is no assessment after an assessment.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: if someone hit another person, they judged the wound deadly, and the victim lived, the striker is exempt. If they judged it deadly and the victim got better, they make a second assessment for money. If he later got worse and died, follow the middle assessment; this is רבי נחמיה. The חכמים say: there is no assessment after an assessment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that spells out the actual argument between רבי נחמיה and the חכמים. It covers a victim who got better and then got worse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees on two points. If the victim fully recovers, the striker is exempt. If he gets better, a new assessment sets the money owed. They argue only when he then gets worse and dies. רבי נחמיה follows the middle assessment, which said he would live, so there is no execution. The חכמים do not allow a second assessment to overturn the first.

keyTerms.meaning: They exempt him
And his condition eased, meaning he got better
A second assessment to set the money owed
The middle assessment
There is no assessment after an assessment

steps.confusionAlert: 'אין אומד אחר אומד' does not help the striker. For the חכמים, the first assessment ('deadly') stands, and the victim's death confirms it.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: One who strikes his fellow,
and they assessed him for death, and he lived,
they exempt him.
If they assessed him for death and he became better than he was,
they assess him a second assessment for money.
And if afterward he got worse and died,
follow the middle assessment,
these are the words of Rabbi Nechemya.

phrases.aramaic: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: אֵין אוֹמֶד אַחַר אוֹמֶד.
phrases.english: And the Sages say: There is no assessment after an assessment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining how each side reads the פסוקים, the גמרא quotes the ברייתא where their practical argument is recorded.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Recovery means exemption, and getting better triggers an assessment for money. If the victim later dies, רבי נחמיה follows the middle assessment, while the חכמים say there is no assessment after an assessment.

steps.title: Another ברייתא: the assessment can move toward life, not toward death
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא teaches that a 'deadly' assessment can be redone toward life, but a 'not deadly' one is never redone toward death. If the victim got better and then died, the striker pays the heirs for damage and pain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: if they judged him for death, they can reassess him for life. If they judged him for life, they do not reassess him for death. If they judged him for death and he got better, they make a second assessment for money. If he later got worse and died, the striker pays damage and pain to the heirs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא. It adds a one-way rule for reassessing and says exactly what the striker pays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A new assessment can only move in the striker's favor, from 'deadly' to 'will live,' and never the other way. When the victim got better and later died, this ברייתא has the striker pay money to the heirs. That points to no execution, in line with following the middle assessment.

keyTerms.meaning: Damage and pain, two of the payments for injuring someone
To the heirs
He got worse

steps.whatToRemember: Reassessment works only in the striker's favor: 'deadly' can become 'will live,' never the reverse. When the victim got better and later died, the second ברייתא has the striker pay the heirs for damage and pain.

phrases.english: It is taught in another one: If they assessed him for death,
they can assess him for life.
If for life, they do not assess him for death.
If they assessed him for death and he became better than he was,
they assess him a second assessment for money,
and if afterward he got worse and died,
he pays damage and pain to the heirs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second ברייתא on the same topic. It adds the one-way reassessment rule and spells out the payment to the heirs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A 'deadly' assessment can be redone toward life, but not the reverse. If the victim got better and then died, the striker pays damage and pain to the heirs.

steps.title: Payment is measured from the moment of the blow
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks from what point the striker's payment is measured. It answers: from the moment he struck the victim.
steps.simpleTranslation: From when does he pay? From the moment that he struck him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from the last step keeps going. It asks a short question and answers it: the striker's payment is figured from the time of the blow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last step said that if the victim got better and then died, the striker pays the heirs for damage and pain. This line tells us which value counts. We measure the victim's loss from the moment he was hit, not from some later point.

keyTerms.meaning: From when? From what point in time?
He pays (money for the damage)
From the moment that he struck him

phrases.english: From when does he pay?
phrases.notes: This means: from what point do we measure the value of the victim's loss for the payment?

phrases.english: From the moment that he struck him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא quoted in step 15 by setting when the payment is measured.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The striker's payment is measured from the moment of the blow.

steps.title: This unattributed ברייתא follows רבי נחמיה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the unattributed ברייתא matches רבי נחמיה's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the unattributed ברייתא is in line with רבי נחמיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells us whose opinion the ברייתא follows. It is רבי נחמיה's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said the striker only pays money when the victim got better and then died. That fits רבי נחמיה, who follows the middle assessment (the improvement). The רבנן say there is no new assessment after an assessment, so for them the striker could still be put to death.

keyTerms.meaning: An unattributed teaching, stated with no name attached
In line with the view of רבי נחמיה

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא that has the striker pay money (and not be executed) when the victim improved and then died follows רבי נחמיה, not the רבנן.

phrases.english: And the unattributed teaching is in line with Rabbi Neḥemya.
phrases.notes: He follows the middle assessment (step 14), so a victim who got better and then died means money, not death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Names whose view the ברייתא of steps 15-16 follows.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ברייתא about payment after improvement follows רבי נחמיה's view of following the middle assessment.

steps.title: משנה: meant to kill someone he would not be executed for, but killed a person he would be
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that if someone meant to kill an animal, a gentile, or a non-viable baby, and instead killed a person, a Jew, or a viable baby, he is exempt from death.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he meant to kill an animal and killed a person, or meant to kill a gentile and killed a Jew, or meant to kill non-viable babies and killed a viable one, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It gives three cases where the killer's target was someone or something he would not be executed for killing, yet he killed someone he would be executed for. In all three he is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To be put to death for murder, the killer must have intended a killing that carries the death penalty. Here his intent was aimed at a target that does not carry that penalty, so the killing he actually did is not counted as a capital murder.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (marks the start of a new משנה)
He intended, he meant to
Babies born unable to survive
A viable person, someone able to live
Exempt (here: from the death penalty)

steps.confusionAlert: Exempt means he is not put to death by בית דין. It does not mean the act was permitted.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
If he intended to kill the animal,
and he killed the person;
to kill the gentile, and he killed a Jew;
phrases.notes: The words "he intended to kill" are understood from the first case.

phrases.english: to kill the non-viable babies, and he killed a viable one –
he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִתְכַּוֵּין לַהֲרוֹג אֶת הַבְּהֵמָה וְהָרַג אֶת הָאָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on intent in murder, separate from the assessment discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who meant to kill a target he would not be executed for, but killed one he would be executed for, is exempt from death.

steps.title: משנה: aimed at the loins, but the blow hit the heart
steps.stepSummary: If he meant to hit the loins with a blow too weak to kill there, but it hit the heart, where it could kill, and the victim died, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he meant to hit him on the loins, and the blow was not strong enough to kill there, but it landed on his heart, where it was strong enough to kill, and he died, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second kind of case. The striker aimed at a body part where his blow could not kill, but it landed where it could kill.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the target is the same person, but the intent was for a blow that could not kill. Since he never intended a deadly blow, he is not executed even though the victim died.

keyTerms.meaning: His loins, the lower back or hips
His heart, meaning the chest over the heart
Enough to kill him

phrases.english: If he intended to strike him on his loins,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא הָיָה בָּהּ כְּדֵי לַהֲמִיתוֹ עַל מׇתְנָיו,
phrases.english: and it was not enough to kill him on his loins,
but it went onto his heart,

phrases.aramaic: וְהָיָה בָּהּ כְּדֵי לַהֲמִיתוֹ עַל לִבּוֹ,
phrases.english: and it was enough to kill him on his heart,
and he died – he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from a wrong target (step 18) to a wrong body part on the same person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A blow aimed where it could not kill, which landed where it could kill, does not bring the death penalty.

steps.title: משנה: the opposite case begins, aimed at the heart
steps.stepSummary: The משנה starts the reverse case, where he meant to hit the heart. The rest continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he intended to strike him on his heart...
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The משנה begins the opposite case, where the striker aimed at the heart, and the ruling comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the striker aims at a place where a blow can kill. The משנה will go on to tell us what happens when the blow lands somewhere else.

keyTerms.meaning: To strike him

phrases.english: If he intended to strike him on his heart

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the reverse of the case in step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ruling for a blow aimed at the heart comes in the next section.
